papers.title_in_file: How many qubits does a machine learning problem require?
papers.what_it_is: A Coherent Computing paper that proves a bit-bit encoded variational quantum classifier can realize any classifier, defines the qubit-count metric Qdataset(x), and measures it on 28 benchmark datasets and on subsets of the Tahoe-100M transcriptomic dataset.

existing.note: The paper gives the exact mean with a confidence interval, the number of datasets, the split and replicates, and the filter that limits the datasets; the stored value says only 27 on average.
existing.value: The authors report that, over 28 benchmark classification datasets (fewer than 1, 000 numeric features, fewer than 10, 000 samples, fewer than 10 classes), split 80% training and 20% testing over 10 replicates, the mean Qdataset under PCA is 27.02 qubits, 95% CI [26.11, 27.94].
quotes: less than 1, 000 features which are all numeric, less than 10, 000 samples, more samples than features, no missing values, single-label classification with less than 10 classes, and no collisions when not encoded. After filtering, we have 28 datasets.
We randomly split each dataset into 80% training and 20% testing, repeated across 10 replicates.
We find the mean Qdataset for the benchmark datasets to be 27.02 qubits, 95% CI [26.11, 27.94].

existing.note: The paper proves two theorems (U* is unitary under condition 3.1; U* is approximable to any accuracy by a finite universal gate set). The step to universal approximation of the underlying function rests on an Observation and on a monotonicity statement the paper calls easy to see, not on a proof. The value now says which parts are proved.
existing.value: The authors state they proved that bit-bit encoding ensures universal approximation. The proved parts are two theorems: the classification operator is unitary, and it can be approximated to any accuracy by a circuit from a finite universal gate set. The step from these to approximating the dataset's underlying function rests on an Observation that each sample needs at most px + py bits, and on the statement that accuracy increases monotonically as bits increase, which the paper says is easy to see.
quotes: We proved that bit-bit encoding inherently ensures universal approximation.
First, we prove that the classification operator U∗ defined in Eq. 2.1 is unitary.
Next, we show that the classification operator U∗ can be approximated to any desired degree of accuracy by a quantum circuit constructed out of a finite universal gate set.
Then each pair (xi, yi) can be uniquely encoded using no more than px + py bits.
Further, it is easy to see that as the number of bits increases, the accuracy of the encoding monotonically increases.
existing.certainty_reason: Theorems 1 and 2 are proved (see the new assertions); the universal approximation step itself is argued, not proved.
existing.reader_inference: The theorems show that any fixed classical classifier on Nx-bit inputs can be realized; that the discretized classifier approaches the true target as bits grow is asserted, not proved.

assertions.value: The paper describes bit-bit encoding: a dimensionality reduction model (PCA by default) is fit on the training set, bits are allocated to each component by its mutual information with the label, the data are min-max normalized and copula transformed, and each value is discretized into bits; the labels map to computational basis states.

assertions.value: The paper takes the correct output for a discretized input that collides with differently labeled samples to be the most frequent label, and defines a linear loss that returns the probability of the model giving the incorrect answer.

assertions.value: The paper defines training coverage as one minus the proportion of training samples with different labels sharing an encoding, testing coverage as one minus the proportion of overlapping test samples not matching the majority training label, and Qdataset(x) as the larger of the qubits needed for training and testing coverage x, plus the class qubits.
quotes: We calculate the training set coverage as 1 − training collision incidence, where the training collision incidence is the proportion of training samples with different class labels which have the same encoding.
where the testing overlap incidence is the proportion of testing samples which overlap with the training data but do not have the same class label as the majority class
The number of qubits required to reach an arbitrary accuracy x is defined as Qdataset(x) = max (Qtrain(x), Qtest(x)) + Qy.

assertions.value: The paper extends bit-bit encoding to a batched streaming mode with several streaming passes (fit dimensionality reduction, compute averaged mutual information scores and per-feature ranges, fit a bin-based copula, re-encode), so collision incidences can be computed for datasets too large for memory.

assertions.value: The authors report training bit-bit encoded models on the first 4 digits of MNIST with exact coordinate updates, after removing collisions; all models converge to the maximum accuracy predicted by bit-bit encoding, larger models need more sweeps, and they show transient accuracy drops attributed to higher-order loss functions.

papers.what_it_is: A proposal and simulation study of an optimization method that repeats a single-ancilla Hadamard test on the cost evolution operator with mid-circuit measurement, keeping the state on the desired outcome and applying an Rx mixer on the undesired one, tested on small vertex cover instances, against QAOA, and on IBM hardware.

selectively protecting the ancilla significantly improves the probability of sampling optimal solutions.

existing.note: The QAOA comparison is on one small vertex cover instance, QAOA at depth 5 with 50 gradient steps against 50 interference steps, and the method's circuits are deeper. They state this convergence is not a pathway to solving NP-hard problems in polynomial time.
